To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) moral judgments are influenced by both action-based and outcome-based values, and that (2) action-based value judgments are associated with the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), and outcome-based value judgments are related to the dorsomedial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortex.

(1) moral judgments are made by two systems, one that represents the value of actions and another that represents the value or outcome of actions, and (2) the systems are distinct in terms of their computational algorithms, neural substrates, and behavioral signatures.

(i) the dual system approach to moral psychology is best characterized in terms of a distinction between outcome- and action-based value representations, (ii) these representations are implemented in distinct brain systems, (iii) these systems interact in a manner consistent with a dual system approach to decision making, and (iv) the interaction of these systems is influenced by individual differences in moral judgment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
understanding moral judgment, moral decision making, and moral behavior from a computational perspective.
the question of how the brain represents and evaluates the moral significance of action, and how this representation relates to the moral significance of outcome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dual system approach to morality has a great deal of potential to provide new insights into the moral psychology of individuals and groups.
dual-systems theories of morality are not well developed.
the dual-system framework for moral psychology is a promising approach, but it is not yet clear which specific version of this approach is best.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have provided a theoretical framework for a dual systems account of morality.
moral cognition is best characterized as the result of two systems that represent value in fundamentally different ways.
the two systems are not "emotional" versus "cognitive," but instead represent action-based versus outcome-based moral judgments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the action-based system can be characterized as a model-free reinforcement learner and the outcome-based system as model-based reinforcement learning.
the dual systems approach to morality is not only compatible with the reinforcement learning framework, but also provides a novel and compelling way to understand the nature of the dual systems.
the two systems are not in opposition but rather complementary, and that the moral domain is an ideal test case for understanding their interaction.
